claims.text: ProductsController carries [Route("api/v1/products")] on the class; List(), marked [HttpGet] with no id, answers the bare collection URL; Get(int id), marked [HttpGet("{id:int}")], answers the item URL.
OrdersController carries [Route("api/v1/orders")] on the class; Create, marked [HttpPost], answers the collection URL; Get(int id), marked [HttpGet("{id:int}")], answers the item URL.
Sending GET /api/v1/products to the running stage-1 lab returns 200 with a JSON array of every product; GET /api/v1/products/1 returns 200 with a single product object, not wrapped in an array.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang stage-1 lab: curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products and /api/v1/products/1

claims.text: By a common REST naming convention, a collection URL usually answers GET (list) and POST (create), and an item URL usually answers GET, PUT or PATCH, and DELETE; HTTP itself attaches no such restriction — it defines each method against whatever URL is the target.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics); REST resource-naming convention independent of any one framework

claims.text: OrdersController has a Cancel(int id) method marked [HttpPatch("{id:int}/cancel")], answering PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel.
A third controller, AuthController, carries [Route("api/v1/auth")] for signing in; it is not a CRUD resource with a plural-noun collection/item pair.
